messages.text: IFRS 16 ka ek simple example bana do, ek junior ko samjhana hai. 3 saal ki office lease, RM 4,000 monthly, discount rate 5%

Theek hai. Pehle lease liability = 36 monthly payments ki present value at 5%/12 monthly. Yeh approx RM 133,300 banti hai. Right-of-use asset bhi initially isi amount pe recognise hoga (agar koi initial direct costs ya incentives nahi). Kya main month-by-month schedule bhi bana doon?
haan schedule chahiye, pehle 6 months kaafi hain

Month 1: opening 133,300, interest 555, payment 4,000, closing 129,855. Month 2: interest 541, closing 126,396. Month 3: interest 527, closing 122,923. Month 4: interest 512, closing 119,435. Month 5: interest 498, closing 115,933. Month 6: interest 483, closing 112,416. ROU asset straight-line depreciate hoga, ~RM 3,703 per month.
perfect. ye excel mein kaise karun bina macro ke
Columns rakho: Month, Opening, Interest (=Opening*5%/12), Payment, Closing (=Opening+Interest-Payment). Next row ka Opening = previous Closing. Opening ka pehla cell =PV(5%/12,36,-4000) se aa jayega.
acha aur Nida ko samjhaun kyun ROU asset aur liability alag alag move karte hain?

Simple line: liability interest ki wajah se front-loaded tareeqe se ghat-ti hai, asset straight-line depreciate hota hai. Isliye shuru ke saalon mein total expense zyada hota hai. Ek chart bana ke dono lines dikhao, junior ko foran samajh aa jata hai.
chart achha idea hai. waise main har Friday 4 baje Nida ke saath ek review session karti hoon, wahan yehi dikhaungi
Achha format hai. Session mein pehle schedule khud banwao, phir chart, phir ek twist: lease modification ya rent-free period. Har hafte ek concept kaafi hai.
rent free period wala twist bhi bana do

Agar pehle 3 months rent-free hain, to payments 33 hongi aur PV kam: approx RM 120,300. Liability aur ROU asset dono isi pe start honge, aur payments month 4 se shuru. Interest pehle 3 months bhi lagta rahega, is liye liability month 3 tak barhti hai.
oh nice ye to tricky hai. ek aur cheez, pivot table mat suggest karna, mujhe nafrat hai unse lol. SUMIFS theek hai
Noted, sirf SUMIFS aur simple formulas. Summary table: =SUMIFS(Interest, Year, 1) waghera, saal-wise interest aur depreciation dikhane ke liye.
bas yehi chahiye tha. shukriya!
Khushi hui. Best of luck with the session!

messages.text: quick q. for a willingness-to-pay study is Van Westendorp enough or do I need conjoint? it's for my MSc thesis on what parents in SEA will pay for kids' reading apps

Van Westendorp is fine if your question is the acceptable price range for one product. Conjoint is better when you want to know how much each feature is worth, like live tutoring versus a parent dashboard. For a master's thesis, Van Westendorp plus a few purchase-intent questions is usually defensible, as long as you discuss its limits.
ok good. I have 412 responses but most came from Quillstep's own parent mailing list. my supervisor already flagged that as sampling bias

That's a fair flag: existing users have already shown they'll pay something. You could recruit a comparison sample through an online panel, or at least compare your sample's demographics to census figures and report the gap.
a panel is out, we're bootstrapping Quillstep and every dollar goes to the product

Then make it a clearly argued limitation. Compare demographics to public data, run the analysis separately for paying and non-paying sign-ups if you have both, and avoid generalising to all parents in the region.
makes sense. Mateo my cofounder keeps telling me to just drop the MSc and focus on the company 🙄 not happening
A lot of founders hear that. Keeping the thesis tightly scoped is the best answer to it: fewer methods, a clear question, and a realistic writing plan.
speaking of scope.. should I add like 10 parent interviews and go mixed methods? or is that scope creep

Interviews would add depth on why parents value certain features, but they need an ethics amendment, recruitment, transcription and coding. With a draft due soon, it's probably scope creep unless your supervisor thinks the survey alone is too thin.
yeah no. survey only, no interviews. decided
Good. Then put your effort into robustness: check the price-point intersections with and without outliers, and report confidence bands.
can you give me a structure for chapter 3

Try: 3.1 Research design and rationale; 3.2 Instrument (Van Westendorp items, purchase intent, demographics); 3.3 Sampling and recruitment, including the mailing-list bias; 3.4 Data cleaning and exclusions; 3.5 Analysis plan; 3.6 Ethics; 3.7 Limitations. Each section can be 400–800 words.
perfect. honestly I only get thesis work done after 11pm these days, daytime is all Quillstep calls 😅
That's a long day. The structure above should let you write in small blocks, one subsection per night. Good luck!

messages.text: explain vesting cliff like im 5

Imagine you get 48 candies for staying four years, one per month. A cliff means you get nothing for the first 12 months, and then on the one-year anniversary you get 12 candies at once. After that, one candy each month. If you leave before a year, you get zero.
lol ok. and what if a cofounder just bails after 6 months, what happens to their shares?

With vesting and a one-year cliff, someone who leaves at six months keeps no vested shares; the company or the other founders can buy back the unvested ones at a nominal price. Without vesting, they would walk away with their full stake. Many founders use four-year vesting with a one-year cliff for exactly this reason.

Sure. Case 1: pH 7.31, PaCO2 30, HCO3 15. What's the primary disorder and is it compensated?
metabolic acidosis, with resp compensation? winter's formula gives 1.5x15+8 = 30.5 so yeah appropriate

Correct. Now the delta ratio: (AG − 12) / (24 − HCO3).
7/9 ≈ 0.78 so mixed high AG + normal AG acidosis?
Yes, a ratio between 0.4 and 0.8 suggests a combined high-AG and normal-AG acidosis, for example DKA with some hyperchloraemia from saline. Want a harder one?

Good that it's sorted. Case 2: pH 7.48, PaCO2 48, HCO3 34, urine chloride 8.

Spot on. Low urine chloride points to vomiting or prior diuretic use, and it responds to saline. Last one: pH 7.25, PaCO2 60, HCO3 26.

Correct: for acute respiratory acidosis HCO3 rises about 1 per 10 rise in CO2, so 26 fits. You're stronger at these than you think.

messages.text: stat mech drill please. GRE style, multiple choice, one at a time

Q1: A system has two energy levels, 0 and ε, each non-degenerate. At temperature T, what is the probability of finding it in the upper level? (A) e^(−ε/kT) (B) 1/(1+e^(ε/kT)) (C) 1/(1+e^(−ε/kT)) (D) ½
B
Correct. Z = 1 + e^(−ε/kT), so P(upper) = e^(−ε/kT)/Z = 1/(1+e^(ε/kT)). Q2: For an ideal monatomic gas, what's the molar heat capacity at constant volume? (A) R/2 (B) R (C) 3R/2 (D) 5R/2
C obviously
Yes, 3R/2 from three translational degrees of freedom. Q3: The Fermi energy of a 3D electron gas scales with number density n as: (A) n^(1/3) (B) n^(2/3) (C) n (D) n^(3/2)
uhh A?
Not quite: it's (B), n^(2/3). k_F scales as n^(1/3) and E_F ∝ k_F², so the exponent doubles. This is a common trap on the test.
argh. ok one more
Q4: Entropy of mixing for two different ideal gases, each one mole, at the same T and P: (A) 0 (B) R ln 2 (C) 2R ln 2 (D) R/2
C
Correct, ΔS = −nR Σ x ln x = 2R ln 2. You're three for four. Your errors are in scaling arguments, so it's worth drilling dimensional reasoning.

That depends on each programme's deadline; many close in December or January, so an April score would usually be too late for this cycle. Better to focus on the next few weeks. Want five more scaling questions?

messages.text: Explain bootstrapping for my MSc class tomorrow in a way that doesn't need heavy maths. They know the CLT.

Try this: we usually have only one sample, but we want to know how much a statistic like the mean would wobble if we could sample again. Bootstrapping pretends our sample is the population: we resample from it with replacement thousands of times, compute the statistic each time, and look at the spread. That spread approximates the sampling distribution, without needing a formula.
nice. quick R snippet they can run in the lab?

x <- c(12, 15, 9, 20, 14, 11, 17)
boot_means <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))
quantile(boot_means, c(0.025, 0.975))
hist(boot_means)
The quantiles give a 95% percentile interval for the mean.
